newsitem.title: INDIA: U.S. balloonist falls short of aim, but sets record.
newsitem.headline: U.S. balloonist falls short of aim, but sets record.

text.p: NONKHAR, India, Jan 20 (Reuter - U.S. adventurer Steve Fossett, haggard but cheerful, landed his balloon in northern India on Monday after a six-day flight which shattered a world record but fell short of his goal of circling the globe.

Fossett told Reuters his "Solo Spirit" touched down near a wheat field at 1:05 p.m. (0735 GMT) about 150 km (95 miles) northwest of Varanasi in Nonkhar town, more than 16,000 km (10,000 miles) from his U.S. starting point.
The 52-year-old commodities broker said that with a bigger balloon, more fuel and some luck he might have completed his bid to fly around the world.
"This is the first time we have seen evidence that it is possible to fly around the world via balloon. Now I didn't make it," said Fossett, speaking near the remote landing site.
"But you can see that we had some good luck in flying to the countries and with a slightly bigger balloon and better fuel supplies, it would be possible to fly around.
"I think that someone will succeed in three years. If I go again, I will have a very good chance."

Witnesses said Fossett, haggard and unshaven, appeared dazed and shivering. But two Indian government doctors who examined him said he faced no health problem. "When we met him he was perfectly healthy and normal," Dr R.P.Tiwari told Reuters.

Villagers said they were frightened as Fossett landed after dropping a gas cylinder. "It was making such a hissing noise that people were naturally frightened," said Devidin Koeri, a village physician near the landing spot.
Police used a rope to roll off the cylinder to a safe spot.
Fosset said villagers who surrounded him were friendly but distracted his attention. "With a hundred people surrounding you, it is not very easy to go about what you want to do."
Earlier on Monday, Fossett told Reuters in Delhi by telephone that he had not made up his mind whether to make another attempt at the around-the-world flight.
"It would require only a few more changes -- a bigger balloon, more fuel and a little bit more luck," he said.
"My team and I have figured out a lot of what it takes to make a successful flight," he said later.
Fossett took off from St Louis, Missouri on January 13, travelling eastward across the Atlantic Ocean and North Africa.

Although he fell short of his dream of being the first balloonist to fly nonstop around the world, he broke the endurance record of six days, 16 minutes for a manned balloon flight, set in 1981 by Americans Ben Abruzzo and Troy Bradley.
On Friday, Fossett broke his own record for balloon distance travel when he passed 8,747 km (5,435 miles) over Algeria. He set the earlier mark on a flight from South Korea to Canada.
Tired after only two hours of sleep each day, Fossett said he had burned more fuel than anticipated over the Atlantic.

He said he had enough fuel to carry on but did not want to fly over the Himalayas, where landing would be dangerous, or into China. "I am sure they wouldn't want me to come and land in their country."
Fossett said he chose to land in India after being "uncertain" about some places in South East Asia.
His balloon snagged a tree when he came down in a field. Hours later, the silvery, deflated balloon could be seen in a heap, still caught in the tree. Some dozen police stood guard.

Fossett told Reuters he would need a day or two to collect his balloon before leaving the area, probably for Delhi. U.S. officials said they hoped the Indian Air Force would fly a helicopter to the site to help Fossett move his gear out.

Before landing, Fossett faced bad weather. "I came across the worst thunder cloud I've ever experienced," he said. "This is the first time that I was forced to fly in a thunderstorm. That is very dangerous."
Project manager Bo Kemper said he believed Fossett would have another go. "You'll see us next year," he said.
